paper_title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: When someone says Thats great, pause or tense expression may reflect sarcasm rather than satisfaction. Understanding emotion requires interpreting words, voice, and visual behavior together, particularly when these cues conflict (Bagher Zadeh et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2026). Misreading them can have consequences beyond an Correspondence to: {max7,bl61,yueg}@illinois.edu. 1 Figure 1: EmoHarness at glance. (a) selected heldout clip (Gemma-4-E4B; Figure 4a): posture suggests neutral, the words negative. Video, Audio (video plus transcript and prosody text), and Shared (the humanwritten scaffold) miss the reference; both MHE harnesses answer negative. (b) Offline, Builder LLM (GPT-5.6 Luna or GPT-6.1 Sol) edits the harness from the frozen students failures and execution traces; checks and validation gates promote edits over four generations. (c) Task-macro Recognition contrasts (VL: Qwen3-VL; Q3.5: Qwen3.5-4B). incorrect label: system may misunderstand persons intent, respond inappropriately to social interaction, or overlook patients indirectly expressed fear or discomfort (Li et al., 2023; Wilf et al., 2023; Han et al., 2026). For smaller multimodal models, transcripts and prosody descriptions supplement visual observations with evidence about what is said and how it is delivered (Cao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026d,b). But interpreting these sources together remains challenging, especially when they suggest different emotions. We therefore ask whether another AI can help small multimodal student use this evidence more effectively without updating the students weights. reinforcement Existing emotion models adapt weights through learning instruction tuning or (Cheng et al., 2024b; Zhao et al., 2025). An alternative is to adapt frozen systems through modelgenerated instructions and program optimization (Zhou et al., 2023; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025). We build on this approach but direct adaptation toward students recurring emotionlabel failures and cross-modal conflicts. We introduce EmoHarness (Figure 1), an AIfor-AI (AI4AI) framework that adapts emotion inference through Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE). An offline Builder examines emotion-label confusions, cross-modal conflicts, and execution traces, and then proposes reusable edits to prompts, execution settings, and restricted verification code. The frozen student organizes visual observations, transcripts, and prosody descriptions into indexed textual evidence, proposes alternative emotional interpretations, and reviews their support and contradictions. Checks and validation select harness that is frozen before evaluation. If no edit passes, the human-written scaffold is retained. The Builder does not answer evaluation questions. To assess the contribution of Builder-guided adaptation, we compare the evolved harness (MHE) with its initial human-written version (Shared) and with single-call prediction from video supplemented with transcripts and prosody descriptions (Audio). Comparing Audio with single-call video-only prediction (Video) measures the effect of adding this audio-derived evidence. We also examine transfer to task types excluded from harness construction and test whether emotion context generated without access to downstream questions helps intent question answering. four

sections.title: Across
sections.content: students and two Builders, EmoHarness improves task-macro Recognition on 5,507 MME-Emotion items by 7.613.4 points over Video. Most of this improvement comes from transcripts and prosody descriptions: Audio outperforms Video by 5.3810.71 points, whereas Builder-guided adaptation produces much smaller changes relative to Shared (0.07 to +0.95 points). Adding the harnesss emotion context also yields small observed gains for three of four students on IntentQA. In summary, we introduce EmoHarness, failure-driven harness construction framework, which boosts frozen multimodal students on emotion recognition and transfers its emotion context to intent question answering. In addition, we conduct systematic analysis of where the boost comes from and what limits harness evolution. We believe our work paves the way for more adaptive and generalizable multimodal systems that can systematically learn from failures, improve without updating model parameters, and transfer acquired capabilities across related tasks.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multimodal emotion understanding. EmotionLLaMA and R1-Omni adapt model weights through instruction tuning and reinforcement learning, respectively (Cheng et al., 2024b; Zhao et al., 2025); EmoHarness instead adapts the inference program around frozen weights. We evaluate on MME-Emotion (Zhang et al., 2026) and reuse emotion context on IntentQA (Li et al., 2023). Following the multi-dimensional evaluation of HEMM (Liang et al., 2024), we separate recognizing an emotion from producing useful downstream context. Optimizing prompts, programs, and harnesses. APE, OPRO, and ProTeGi search instructions with model-generated proposals or feedback (Zhou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Pryzant et al., 2023); DSPy and MIPRO optimize multi-stage programs (Khattab et al., 2024; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024); TextGrad and Trace learn from textual feedback and execution traces (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2026); and ADAS and AFlow search code-defined agents (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Meta-Harness exposes prior code, scores, and traces to proposer (Lee et al., 2026), automated harness adaptation can target the failures of smaller models (Yang et al., 2026), and multi-agent and self-evolving systems learn from feedback (Li et al., 2025, 2026c,a). MHE applies this line of work to multimodal emotion recognition: students emotion confusions and cross-modal conflicts drive reusable edits, separate validation split gates every promotion, and 2 the evolved harness is frozen and reused, unlike programs generated for each request (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023). Feedback and procedural adaptation. SelfRefine revises single outputs and Reflexion carries feedback across trials (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023); EmoHarness separates the students per-instance review from the Builders offline edits. Self-correction can fail (Huang et al., 2024), agent errors can cascade across steps (Zhu et al., 2025), and explanations need not reflect decisions (Turpin et al., 2023). We therefore score harnesses only on items the Builder never saw, report validation and evaluation gains separately, and count student calls (Kapoor et al., 2025).

sections.content: Given video v, request q, and allowed labels Yq, harness invokes the frozen student Mθ and returns labels ˆY , an explanation z, and trace τ : ( ˆY , z, τ ) = H(Mθ; v, (v), q, Yq). (1) Fixed preprocessing (v) supplies transcript, prosodic descriptors, and frame cache. MHE changes but never θ, and within the perception tools, evidence and output schemas, and output controller are also fixed; the Builder may rewrite prompts, settings (e.g., transcript presentation), and restricted verification code.

sections.title: 3.2 Evidence-Indexed Emotion Inference
sections.content: Audio preprocessing uses Whisper large-v3 (via faster-whisper) and openSMILE eGeMAPSv02 (Radford et al., 2023; Eyben et al., 2010, 2016); reference-normalized acoustic features become descriptions such as high pitch, never emotion labels. The human-written scaffold H0 (Shared) uses four student calls. Observe extracts facial, bodily, scene, and temporal cues from the video, decoded at 2 fps; deterministic assembly indexes them (v1, v2, . . .) along with transcript sentences and prosody phrases (a1, a2, . . .), and later calls see only this textual record. Propose lists candidate labels with confidences and with identifiers of supporting and contradicting evidence; deterministic code checks the identifiers against the record and then ranks the candidates. Review re-examines the ranked candidates, and its output is verified the same way. fixed controller then selects at most three labels from the vocabulary. It prefers candidates whose valid support exceeds their contradiction and fills any remaining slots from the ranking, so it always returns an answer, even one without valid support. Explain then writes an explanation that cannot change the labels. Each malformed call may be retried once, under cap of six calls (Appendix B).

sections.title: 3.3 Meta-Harness Evolving
sections.content: MHE evolves the harness over = 4 generations. In each, the Builder proposes candidate edits, and gates either promote one candidate or keep the current harness. MHE inherits from Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) proposer that reads prior harness code and execution traces. It differs in three respects. First, the Builder sees the failures of one frozen student, clustered by goldprediction confusion and by cross-modal conflict; deterministic check flags conflict when the students visual and audio-derived citations favor different labels. Second, gates on separate validation split decide promotion, and the Builder sees neither validation scores nor gate decisions, only the resulting harness. Third, each run keeps one current harness, the incumbent, giving chain H0 HT . Variation. The incumbent runs on construction split Db, whose failures the Builder may read. Given the incumbents files, intermediate records, clustered failures, and earlier proposals with check and reviewer feedback, the Builder proposes up to four candidate harnesses, each an edit aimed at one failure cluster; evaluation data are never exposed. Selection. Candidates must pass file-scope, schema, loadability, and static-code checks, as well as proposal reviewer that rejects, for example, edits that force label regardless of evidence or add unsupported settings; these are filters, not guarantees. Survivors run on the validation split Dv. Let ri(H) [0, 1] be per-item Recognition (Section 4.2) and St the validation items solved (ri = 1) by any incumbent so far. sections.title: 4.1 Students, Builders, and Data
sections.content: Models. We serve Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL4B (Bai et al., 2025), Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), and Gemma-4-E4B (Gemma Team, 2026) with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) at temperature zero, with thinking disabled for Qwen3.5 and Gemma. Audio reaches every student only as transcript and prosody text. Each students harness is evolved separately by GPT-5.6 Luna and by GPT-6.1 Sol; each Builder also acts as its own proposal reviewer, and GPT-5.6 Luna scores the reasoning proxy. Each studentBuilder pair has one four-generation run. third Builder configuration, which changes no conclusion, is described in Appendix A. 4 Data. Construction and validation use 399 and 394 MME-Emotion items (Zhang et al., 2026) from three task types (ER-Lab, ER-Wild: lab and in-thewild emotion recognition; SA: sentiment analysis). Evaluation uses 5,507 further items, namely the benchmark minus every item whose media overlap construction, validation, or reserved 129-item set. The evaluation set contains 2,963 items in the seen types and 2,544 in five held-out types (noisy, fine-grained, and multi-label emotion recognition: Noise-ER, FG-ER, ML-ER; fine-grained sentiment: FG-SA; intent recognition: IR). Heldout refers to task type, not to an untouched test set: 986 evaluation items, which we cannot identify, were inspected during development. Inspection could have influenced any human design choice, most plausibly the scaffold, but not the Builders edits directly: the Builder never saw evaluation items (Appendix A).

sections.title: 4.2 Conditions and Metrics
sections.content: Video prompts the student once with the video, and Audio adds transcript and prosody text to that call. Shared runs the four-call scaffold H0, and MHE runs the frozen evolved harness . Recognition, computed locally without an LLM judge, scores the first normalized prediction for single-label requests and the fraction of gold labels recovered for multi-label requests, recall-like score that ignores extra labels. AudioVideo measures added evidence, and MHEShared measures what evolution adds. SharedAudio mixes four changes: multi-step procedure, four calls instead of one, later calls that see only text record of the video, and more predicted labels, which the recall-like score rewards. sections.title: Changes
sections.content: Figure 4 follows two Gemma-4-E4B items. In (a), Shared rates mildly negative remark as strong negative because confidence score, not an observed cue, ranks that label first. With the GPT-5.6 Luna edit, the review call treats the composed posture as evidence for neutral reading, and the harness answers the reference negative instead. In (b), Video answers the correct Neutral, but once the transcript of billing complaint is added, Audio, Shared, and both MHE harnesses answer Frustration. The GPT5.6 Luna harness keeps Frustration even though its added rule asks it to treat neutral as serious alternative: its explanation never names Neutral and still lists crossed arms that no sampled frame shows. Over all 5,507 items, this harness changes Shareds label set on 169 items: 46 improve, 45 worsen, and 78 score the same (more cases in Appendix F).

sections.title: 5.4 RQ3: Does Emotion Context Help Intent
sections.content: QA? On IntentQA, AudioFrames ranges from 2.06 to +3.28 points  (Table 2)  . Adding the emotion context raises accuracy in all six pairs of Qwen3-VL8B, Qwen3-VL-4B, and Gemma-4-E4B (+0.23 to +1.87 points; Figure 5, Appendix Figure 10); for Qwen3-VL-4B both pointwise intervals exclude zero (+1.87 [+0.47, +3.27]; +1.50 [+0.05, +2.97]). Qwen3.5-4B loses 1.50 and 1.41 points. Each context changes the correctness of 248 to 306 of the 2,134 answers, so each net change is small difference between many gains and losses. None of the eight contrasts survives Holm correction (smallest adjusted = .085; Appendix Table 5), and the mean change is positive in every official question type, none significantly (Appendix Table 6). We have no length-matched control (Appendix G), so longer inputs, rather than emotion content, could account for these changes. Scaffold contexts exist only for Qwen3.5-4B, whose GPT-5.6 Luna harness retained the scaffold. Its GPT-6.1 Sol context matches the scaffolds for 531 of 567 videos. No experiment therefore compares scaffold context with substantively evolved one, so these changes cannot be attributed to evolution.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: When does MHE help? The largest gain, GPT5.6 Luna on Qwen3-VL-4B, occurs for the only student whose scaffold scores below Audio. Its edits add 0.95 points, mostly on held-out types (+1.24 versus +0.47 on seen types). They change the label set on 1,189 items (21.6%): 281 improve, 233 worsen, and 675 score the same. Three findings suggest why the other gains are small. First, each promotion picks the best of up to four candidates on 394 items, so the winners validation gain tends to overstate its gain on new items (Section 5.1). The Recognition gate also requires no margin: three of the eleven promotions rest on single validation item (0.25 points). Second, the regression gate blocked every large validation gain for both Builders: all twelve candidates that gained at least eight validation items (2.03 points) exceeded the 5% regression budget. Nine were for Qwen3.5-4B, whose prompt edits change the correctness of 56 construction items on average, against 2327 for the other students. Third, the other evolved harnesses are conservative: each changes the label set on fewer than 4% of evaluation items. The regression gate protects solved cases at the cost of broad edits; whether looser gate generalizes better needs separate test set. Edits are instructions the student may not follow. In Figure 4a the added rule moves the trace toward neutral alternative. In Figure 4b the rule written for the NeutralFrustration confusion is ignored: Neutral is never named. These selected cases suggest that the students instruction following, not only the Builders proposals, can limit what edits achieve. sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Evidence base. The media-overlap filter that defines the evaluation split was applied once and has not been independently re-verified. Part of the evaluation set was inspected during development, so held-out results describe unseen task types rather than an untouched test set. The 129 reserved ex8 nition separately on items with cross-modal conflicts, so whether edits help where they are aimed is untested. Valid citations do not establish grounding or faithful explanations, fallback logic can complete unsupported answers, and static checks and model reviewers do not guarantee correct verification code. The 64-token answer cap leaves some downstream replies unparsed, and Qwen3.5-4B instead answers under 1,024-token cap with finalanswer parser, so answer formatting differs across students.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Benchmark emotion labels are interpretations of behavior, not direct measurements of private mental states or clinical conditions. This work does not validate use in diagnosis, employment screening, surveillance, or educational assessment. Cultural, linguistic, and demographic variation requires separate analysis with suitable annotations. Dataset access and redistribution must follow source terms. Videos, transcripts, and construction diagnostics may identify individuals; external model processing and released traces must respect applicable permissions, and the frames reproduced in our casestudy figures come from public research datasets, with on-screen names removed. We use MMEEmotion (MIT license) and IntentQA (whose repository states no license) for non-commercial research evaluation only; source videos remain subject to their original terms. The student models are released under Apache 2.0, and Whisper and faster-whisper (MIT), openSMILE (audEERING research license), and vLLM (Apache 2.0) are used under their terms. We release no new data.

sections.title: G Controls for Future Work
sections.content: The controls below would sharpen the comparisons in this paper. Evidence and computation. Transcript-only and prosody-only conditions would separate the sources of the audio gain. one-call structured prediction using the same tools and controller would test decomposition against direct call that uses the same output contract. Repeated direct samples with fixed aggregation rule would test the value of additional calls. Token and call counts must be measured rather than presumed matched. Giving the decision stages access to the media would measure how much information is lost when observations are converted to text. Construction and context. Comparing promptor configuration-only search with full-bundle 17 search requires matched splits and budgets. Evaluating the twelve candidates that the regression gate rejected despite gains of at least eight validation items, or rerunning selection with looser δ, would test whether the gate rather than the proposals limits MHE. Independent construction repetitions are necessary to assess search variability. Sharedgenerated contexts for every student are needed to test the downstream increment from evolution. Length-matched visual captions and non-emotion summaries would separate emotion-specific utility from generic additional text. The reserved examples require separately frozen evaluation, and explanation quality requires its own measurement.
